items.title: Texas governor-elect wants a data center moratorium: ~13GW exposed, ~$650B of capex at $50B/GW
items.idea: Democrats took House and Senate, and governors in Texas, Ohio, Georgia and Pennsylvania, the states with the most planned gigawatts. Gina Hinojosa (TX) wants a statewide moratorium on new data centers until the legislature writes rules. One research firm puts ~13GW of Texas capacity directly exposed; at ~$50B capex per GW that is ~$650B. NBC: 76% oppose data centers in their community; 45 local ballot measures, 33 on one count restrict development; several Ohio cities banned facilities above 25MW.
items.angle: Power and permitting were already the bottleneck; now they are a political variable with a date (Jan 2027). Pair with neocloud/BDC credit exposure and gas turbine and grid names.
items.tweetA: 13GW exposed in Texas alone. At $50B a gigawatt that's a $650B question mark sitting on one governor's first-100-days list. The AI capex debate just moved from 'is there demand' to 'is there a permit'. $VST $CEG $NRG
items.tweetB: Ohio cities banning anything above 25MW is the detail to remember. That's smaller than one training cluster rack row at scale. Retail voters just set a de facto cap on campus size, and nobody has modeled it.

items.title: Elon spent ~$445M on the midterms, $200M+ in Texas, and lost Texas anyway
items.idea: Musk spent about $445M backing Republicans, the most of any donor in US history, with 200M+ in Texas. Talarico beat Paxton for Senate by 12+ points and Hinojosa beat Abbott. Ohio and Michigan spending also fell short. Parekh notes it is under 0.5% of his net worth. Tesla and SpaceX are reportedly weighing a merger into a $3T+ company.
items.angle: Political capital of tech founders is now a liability variable for gov-contract revenue (SpaceX, xAI). Watch the merger narrative against a hostile Congress.
items.tweetA: $445M bought Elon zero Texas. The interesting part isn't the money, it's that the most expensive Senate race ever was lost by 12. If you're underwriting SpaceX/Tesla government revenue, there is now an oversight committee with subpoena power in your model.
items.tweetB: Tech donors outspent everyone ($600M by Big Tech, $445M by one man) and the electorate treated it as a negative signal. First cycle where being the billionaire in the room costs votes. Expect the lobbying playbook to go quiet and local.

items.title: Federal preemption of state AI laws 'looks gone for good'; hearings for tech CEOs coming
items.idea: Citing The Verge and Axios: with gavels in Congress, Democrats can launch investigations and call tech executives to testify. The push to override state AI laws looks dead. Axios frames the result as an 'AI earthquake' with dozens of data center moratoriums approved. Parekh notes big tech's political pragmatism (accommodating the administration) is now the exposure.
items.angle: State-by-state AI regulation patchwork becomes the base case; compliance cost favors scaled incumbents.
items.tweetA: The federal preemption bill was the bull case for 'one rulebook'. It's dead. 50 state AI regimes plus county-level data center zoning is the new base case, and only the hyperscalers can afford the lawyers.
items.tweetB: Meta hedged before the vote, Apple/Google/MSFT accommodated for a year. Hearings in January will ask what they traded for it. Sell-side models have a zero in the 'political risk' line.

items.title: OLED iPad mini starts at $699, up from $499: Apple pricing power on A20 Pro
items.idea: New 8.5in OLED mini on the A20 Pro (~50% faster), water resistant, but 60Hz, no Face ID. Starting price $699 vs $499 previous. Full chip tier is about $1,000; nano-texture requires more storage so effectively $900. MKBHD calls it the most Apple product ever, the price ladder is the point.
items.angle: A 40% entry price hike on a mature product line is a read on Apple pricing power and memory/OLED cost pass-through.
items.tweetA: Apple raised the entry price of the iPad mini 40% in one generation, from $499 to $699, and reviewers are complaining about 60Hz, not the price. That's pricing power. Memory costs are being passed straight to the consumer. $AAPL
items.tweetB: A 5.5in phone that unfolds to 7.5in, plus a $699 mini. Apple is quietly turning the screen-size ladder into a margin ladder. The product line is now price discrimination by storage tier.

items.title: SPY gapped +1.15% after the midterms: second-largest post-midterm open since 1993
items.idea: Only 1998 (+1.27%) was bigger. SPY rose the next day after 7 of 8 prior midterms (range +0.17% in 1994 to +2.14% in 2018; 2022 was -2.06%). Closest analogs, where both chambers flipped against the president: 1994 and 2006. Both finished day one at about +0.2%, but the following month was -4.17% (1994) versus +1.84% (2006).
items.angle: The day-one pop is nearly uninformative about the month. The fork is macro (1994 hiking cycle vs 2006 plateau), which is the Ironsides/Citrini debate.
items.tweetA: Everyone will quote 'stocks rise after midterms'. The two cleanest analogs, 1994 and 2006, both closed day one at +0.2% and then diverged by 6 points over the next month: -4.2% vs +1.8%. The election doesn't pick the path. The Fed does.
items.tweetB: Second-biggest midterm gap in 33 years, with CTAs short 26 sessions in a row. That's not a vote of confidence, it's a short squeeze with a political excuse. Different trade, different exit.

items.title: Banks stuck with $15B of funded bridge loans on an Anthropic-backed Texas data center halted by the DC moratorium
items.idea: Citrini says banks got hung on $15B funded bridge loans to a datacenter project halted by the Texas moratorium, and credit markets not backstopped by hyperscalers have ground to a halt: neoclouds, high yield private credit, BDCs. Hyperscaler annualized capex is about to hit $1T; combined market cap is over $10T, and they can no longer fund from cash flow. Turbine backorders and interconnect delays create 'takeout risk' and 'completion defaults' when completion dates collide with debt maturities.
items.angle: The first real AI-capex credit event is a construction-finance problem, not a revenue problem. Look at who holds the bridge paper.
items.tweetA: $15B of funded bridge loans on a data center that now can't be built. That is the first chapter of the AI credit story, and it's about permits, not demand. Banks that can't syndicate it keep it. Watch bank earnings footnotes and BDC marks.
items.tweetB: Hyperscalers: $10T market cap, can't self-fund capex, issuing debt AND equity into a market with fewer willing buyers. Each deal drains liquidity from the next. The bottleneck stopped being silicon and became the marginal buyer.

items.title: 'Peak capex growth': ecosystem ARR at least $200B against ~$1T annualized capex, RPO growth at multi-year lows
items.idea: Quarterly RPO growth has slowed to the lowest level in years, and the labs have slowed commitments (the peak of 'mega commitments' is behind us). Ecosystem ARR is at least $200B, but doubling capex would require revenue with a starting unit of 'trillion'. Citrini's call: asymmetric risk is now to the downside, 'a coda not a stop', and they overhauled the Citrindex toward reversals, pairs and fresh ideas. Since inception on 5/31/23 the Citrindex beat SPX by over 2.5x.
items.angle: A thematic shop that rode the AI trade for three years declaring the end of 'the Trade as we know it' is itself a sentiment marker.
items.tweetA: $200B ARR is a number nobody predicted in 2023 and it's still one-fifth of annualized capex. Sequoia's $600B question now has a trillion-dollar sequel. Peak growth in capex, not peak AI.
items.tweetB: When the best thematic book of the cycle (2.5x SPX) tears up its own portfolio and says 'reversals and pairs', that's not a bear call, it's a regime tell. Same people called the entry in May 2023.

items.title: OpenAI's July 30 token price cut: price war, commoditization, and Anthropic's share 'immediately flowed'
items.idea: Citrini says OpenAI slashed token prices on July 30 and it worked: Anthropic's growth hit a wall as share flowed to OpenAI. Customers were price elastic given near-identical products and frictionless, often automated switching. Prices have since stabilized; Anthropic's S-1 (published last week) was cleaner than expected and the company is cash-flow positive early. Price wars mark 'the beginning of the end of the great railroad cycle'.
items.angle: Switching costs are the whole terminal value debate. If routing is automated, API revenue behaves like a commodity.
items.tweetA: One price cut moved share between the two biggest labs. That's your answer on switching costs: near zero. A business whose customers are routers can't have pricing power, and the S-1 multiples assume it does.
items.tweetB: Railroads, fiber, now tokens. Every one of them had real demand and real capex and a price war right before the equity cycle peaked. The question is whether July 30 was the war or the first skirmish.

items.title: Job-creation breakeven fell from 155k (2023-24) to 85k (2025) to 5-10k by late 2026 as net immigration turns negative
items.idea: Citing the Fed Board's Murray-Vidangos series, breakeven payroll growth is 5-10k by late 2026. Payrolls are running 51k on a 3-month basis and 68k YTD, so the labor market is absorbing supply at or above breakeven despite 'anemic' headlines. Citrini also notes job openings are rising for the first time in four years, with strength in cyclical manufacturing.
items.angle: Headline NFP is the wrong yardstick; the unemployment rate and wages carry the signal. This frames Friday's payrolls print.
items.tweetA: Breakeven payrolls went from 155k to 5-10k in three years. A 51k print is now a boom by that measure. We are grading the labor market on a curve that no longer exists.
items.tweetB: Cutting immigration lowers breakeven, tightens wages, keeps services inflation sticky. The policy and the Fed's 'inflation-first' stance are the same trade viewed from two ends.

items.title: 9 of 14 asset pairs in the Regime Cube trade 'stagflationary'; cyclicals vs defensives -6.9% in six months
items.idea: Growth and inflation gauges say inflationary growth, but asset-price behavior and 10-year real yields push toward stagflation. Cyclicals vs defensives is down 2.4% in a month, 2.9% in three, 6.9% in six. The Nasdaq fell 8% from highs in October, but underneath it was a 'bloodbath' as leveraged long/short trades unwound. Factor crowding now matters like 0DTE did for the S&P. Low beta has only just begun to outperform.
items.angle: The market is pricing late-cycle while the data says expansion. That gap is the trade.
items.tweetA: Data says inflationary growth. Cross-asset pairs say stagflation. When the gauge and the price disagree, one of them reprices. Nine of fourteen pairs already did.
items.tweetB: Defensives winning for six months while PMIs sit at multi-year highs is what late cycle looks like. The only question is whether you chase staples at nosebleed multiples or keep paying for beta.

items.title: Walleye -5.9% in October (worst since March 2020), down 9 of 10 months in 2026; Citadel keeps winning
items.idea: Per With Intelligence, Walleye Opportunities Fund fell 5.9% in October and is -6.6% YTD; its only positive month was +4% in April. Since early 2024 Citadel's AUM barely moved while Millennium, Point72, Balyasny, Schonfeld, Walleye, Verition and ExodusPoint grew ~$100B (+60%, ~80% with Millennium's $22B raise). Ghose focuses on return volatility, which is not what a multi-manager promises.
items.angle: Pod-shop capacity grew 60% into a crowded factor book; October's unwind is the test. Fits Citrini's long/short unwind.
items.tweetA: Walleye: -5.9% in a month and down nine of ten this year. That's not a pod shop, that's a levered factor bet with a risk manager. Pod AUM +60% since 2024 while Citadel stayed flat. Citadel's the only one that ran the capacity discipline.
items.tweetB: A +4% month and a -5.9% month in the same year from a multi-manager. The product is supposed to be bond-like vol. If the pods deleverage together the same October unwind hits the factor longs from the other side.

items.title: K-shaped labor market driving wage disinflation while the Fed keeps a December hike alive
items.idea: Ironsides expects modest October payrolls and weighs wages over surveys distorted by population estimates and immigration. The lowest-income workers' brief relative wage gains have reversed; small-business employment is historically weak; September's JOLTS small-business openings surge is not trusted. Post-midterm risks: budget fights and next summer's debt-ceiling deadline pushing term premium up. They favor lower policy rates, shorter issuance, looser bank capital rules, and compare 2018 as the market analog.
items.angle: Hawkish Fed plus disinflating wages plus a debt ceiling date: a different path than Citrini's wage-support story. Two views of the same labor market.
items.tweetA: Citrini says labor is tight enough to support wages. Ironsides says wages are disinflating and the bottom of the distribution is rolling over. Both can't be right. Friday's average hourly earnings by income decile is the tiebreaker.
items.tweetB: The 2018 analog: relief rally, Fed still hiking, credit spreads the thing that finally stops it. If a December hike stays live into a debt-ceiling fight, you want to be watching HY OAS, not the Nasdaq.

items.title: Brent -10% to below $100 on the idea that a Democratic Congress constrains the Iran war
items.idea: Innes argues Democrats can use upcoming funding deadlines as leverage to rein in the Iran war and some tariffs. S&P +1.5% (best session since August), megacap tech +3%, Treasury yields fell across the curve, the dollar had its sharpest drop in two months, Bitcoin recovered toward $80K. Oil is the real signal: 'the bond and oil markets gave a more useful signal than political commentary.' He flags that Trump still holds the veto pen and Gulf diplomacy has burned markets before.
items.angle: A war premium being repriced by US domestic politics. That is a new transmission channel for oil.
items.tweetA: Brent fell 10% because American voters might defund a war. That's not a supply story. If the risk premium is political, the hedge isn't a barrel, it's the House calendar. Funding deadlines are now oil catalysts.
items.tweetB: Same election, opposite readings in 24 hours: Tuesday 'Democrats are risk-off', Wednesday 'Democrats are disinflationary'. The market only needed oil to move to flip the narrative. $XLE $USO

items.source: Stephen Innes / The Dark Side of the Boom
items.title: Post-midterm S&P: +14.1% average over six months since 1970 vs +5.7% in non-midterm periods, every one positive
items.idea: Innes cites that every post-midterm six-month window since 1970 was positive, averaging 14.1% vs 5.7% in comparable non-midterm periods, and positions the S&P 8,000 path as still open given non-euphoric positioning after the tech selloff. Conditions: oil lower, yields cooperating, AI correction a valuation reset not an earnings problem.
items.angle: Seasonality is the one thing everyone will cite this week. Use it as a crowded-narrative flag.
items.tweetA: 'Every post-midterm six months since 1970 was positive.' True. It's also a statistic with about fifteen data points and a Fed that was not hiking in most of them. Don't size a trade on it.
items.tweetB: The bull case for the next six months leans on three things: oil, yields, AI earnings. The election itself isn't one of them.

items.source: Stephen Innes / The Dark Side of the Boom
items.title: Gold's 3.7% Friday plunge: forced liquidation, now below Bloomberg's fair-value model for the first time since 2023
items.idea: Simon White's model (real yields, dollar, S&P 500, copper YoY) now has gold below fair value for the first time since 2023, after a 185% rally. The plunge came as semis had their 41st-worst session in 30+ years and CTAs flipped. US gold ETF holders have not capitulated, while Asia-domiciled gold ETFs did not sell even as US ETFs saw outflows. ETFs are only 1.8% of above-ground gold.
items.angle: Gold selling as an ATM for margin calls: a cross-asset liquidity signal, not a gold signal.
items.tweetA: Yields down, dollar down, gold -3.7%. That's not gold, that's somebody's margin call. When a hedge sells off alongside the risk it hedges, liquidity is the thing being priced. First time below fair value since 2023.
items.tweetB: ETFs are 1.8% of above-ground gold. Everyone watches US ETF flows while Asia held through the drawdown. The marginal holder at these prices doesn't have a ticker.

items.title: Big Tech spent ~$600M on the midterms and the anti-AI side won anyway; 130+ Democrats ran anti-tech ads
items.idea: More than 130 Democratic candidates ran anti-tech ads (Semafor). Big Tech spent ~$600M, and the leading pro-AI super PAC network started with $100M (FT). OpenAI pivoted to 'compute campuses' and community input, met with skepticism. The article frames three gates the industry needs open: public subsidies, state/local siting approvals, and utility rules on who pays for grid capacity. Counter-case: security argument vs China, and funded projects can relocate to friendlier states.
items.angle: 'Who pays for the grid' is the policy variable. Tariff design (large-load tariffs) is where margin is decided.
items.tweetA: $600M of spending and the issue still won. The backlash isn't about models or China, it's about electricity bills. Large-load tariffs are the real AI policy now, and almost nobody models them.
items.tweetB: OpenAI renamed data centers 'compute campuses'. A rebrand doesn't change who pays for the substation. The next fight is ratepayer protection clauses, and developers who pre-sign them will get permits faster.

items.title: Uber: during its busiest week last quarter, only four people booked a ride using an AI agent
items.idea: TechCrunch reports Uber says four people booked rides through an AI agent in its busiest week of the quarter.
items.angle: Agentic commerce adoption versus the narrative. Four is a rounding error on tens of millions of weekly trips.
items.tweetA: Four. During Uber's busiest week. Agents were supposed to be the new front door to every consumer app. The distribution shift everyone is pricing hasn't shown up in the one workflow that should be easiest.
items.tweetB: Contrast: a16z says software stops being the moat and the network is. Uber's network, not any agent interface, is still doing 100% of the work. The agent layer has to earn its place first.

items.title: Vance blames the Iran war for GOP midterm losses; Trump backs Hegseth; polls missed the wave by more than 2016
items.idea: Items from the 'Things happen' section: JD Vance said the Iran war, not immigration, explains Republican losses (The Hill). Trump is standing behind War Secretary Hegseth despite insider criticism (Fox). Axios reports the polling miss was bigger than 2016's miss on Republicans. Jeffries launched his bid for speaker.
items.angle: The administration itself is naming the war as a political cost, which raises the odds of a negotiated off-ramp and ties to oil falling.
items.tweetA: When the Vice President says the war cost you the House, the war has an expiry date. Oil figured that out in a day. Brent doesn't need a ceasefire, it needs the political cost to be public.
items.tweetB: Polls missed Democrats by more than they missed Republicans in 2016. Every model that used polls as a prior for policy risk was off, and so were prediction markets that priced them.

items.title: CTAs at -3.3 standard deviations on US equities, short 26 consecutive sessions
items.idea: Citadel's CTA model: aggregate US equity positioning at -3.3σ, below the 2nd percentile of its one-year range, 10th percentile since 2018, lowest since March 31. It fell from +1.7σ three months ago to -1.0σ one month ago. The setup improves into November per the headline.
items.angle: Fuel for a squeeze: the post-election rally may be mostly systematic buyers covering.
items.tweetA: CTAs went from +1.7σ to -3.3σ in three months and were short 26 sessions straight. A 1.5% rally on an election headline in that positioning is a cover, not a conviction. Watch what happens when the shorts are done.
items.tweetB: Positioning at -3.3σ while the bank strategists were warning of a risk-off event. The people who needed to sell had sold two weeks ago. Narrative lagged the flow again.

items.title: Brent down 19.6% in three days, the biggest such move since April 2020
items.idea: Quoting @kevrgordon: 'Brent crude is down by 19.6% in the past three days. We haven't seen a move like that since April 2020.'
items.angle: Pair with the Innes thesis. Sets up a refiner and shale equity re-rating, and the inflation-breakeven repricing.
items.tweetA: Brent -19.6% in three days. Last time was April 2020 and that was demand collapsing. This time demand is fine and it's a risk premium evaporating. Those are very different trades for the next month.
items.tweetB: A 20% oil move and energy stocks at 5% of members above their 20DMA while everything else is above. Equities already priced the crash. The question is whether crude does a round trip if the Gulf headline flips.

items.title: ADP: private payrolls +86k in October, matching September; gains across all firm sizes two months running
items.idea: ADP showed 86k jobs added in October, equal to September's total, with firms of all sizes adding jobs for the second consecutive month.
items.angle: Strong enough to keep the December hike debate alive; weak vs historical norms but above the new breakeven (see Citrini).
items.tweetA: 86k on ADP, two months in a row, across all firm sizes. With breakeven at roughly 5-10k, that's a labor market running hot. Ironsides says small business is weak. ADP says otherwise.
items.tweetB: The Fed's chart on breakeven is the one that matters. 86k against a 5-10k breakeven means unemployment falls, wages firm and December stays live.

items.title: Energy and Tech correlation turned negative as the top two S&P sectors: first reading since at least 1973
items.idea: As of October 28, when Energy and Tech were the top two performing S&P 500 sectors, the correlation between them was negative, the first such reading in NDR's data going back to 1973. Separately, nine sectors have 70%+ members above the 20DMA, the exceptions being Energy (5%) and Tech (29%).
items.angle: Dispersion regime: two stocks groups with opposite macro sensitivities (oil up is bad for tech via yields) leading together is a 'barbell' that unwinds on one headline, which is what just happened with oil.
items.tweetA: First negative correlation between the two best sectors in 50+ years. Energy and Tech led for opposite reasons: war and AI. Brent -20% kills one leg in three days. That was the pair trade nobody knew they were running.
items.tweetB: Breadth is 9 sectors above 70% of members over the 20DMA, with Energy at 5% and Tech at 29%. The index rally this week is a rotation into everything you didn't own, funded by your two winners.

items.title: Securities services: real-time settlement and agentic AI reshape custody economics
items.idea: Thin email: only a blurb. McKinsey's Banking Practice leaders (Ishaan Seth, Stephanie Hauser) promote 'Rewiring securities services for a new era of competition and growth', saying disruptive forces, from real-time settlement to agentic AI, are changing the dynamics of the industry. Also listed: 'Anchor or drift: wallet share in 2026' and 'Creating value through agentic-enabled capital origination'. Body analysis is in the linked article, not in the email.
items.angle: Financial plumbing: T+0 settlement and tokenized collateral compress custody fee pools. Worth reading for custodian exposure.
items.tweetA: Custody was a fee on friction. Real-time settlement removes the friction. McKinsey is now writing 'rethink growth priorities' for securities services, which is how consultants say the fee pool is shrinking. $BK $STT
items.tweetB: Agentic AI at the back office plus T+0 is a double hit to custodians' ops margin and float income. The winner is whoever owns the collateral rails, not the ledger.
